title: Hola: greetings and introducing yourself
objective: You can greet someone and write a simple introduction giving your name and where you're from.

explanation.markdown:
Spanish uses **ser** to say who you are and where you're from. It changes with the subject: *yo soy* ("I am"), *tú eres* ("you are"), *él/ella es* ("he/she is"). So: *Soy Ana* ("I'm Ana"), *Soy de México* ("I'm from Mexico"), *Ella es de Colombia* ("She's from Colombia").

Spanish usually drops the subject pronoun — *Soy de México* sounds more natural than *Yo soy de México*, though both are correct.

To give your name, learn *me llamo…* ("my name is…") as a set phrase: *me llamo Ana*. Its inner machinery comes much later; for now just memorize *me llamo / te llamas / se llama*.

One caution: don't confuse *el* ("the") with *él* ("he") — the accent changes the meaning.

acceptedEs: hasta luego
muchas gracias
disculpa
discúlpame
mi nombre es
tu nombre es
su nombre es
Hola, yo soy Ana.
¡Hola! Soy Ana.
¡Hola! Yo soy Ana.
hints: Start with the greeting, then say who you are with the *yo* form of 'to be.'
'To be' here is *ser*; in the *yo* form it becomes *soy*. Add your name after it.
*Hola, ___ Ana* — fill in the *yo* form of *ser*.
Use the word for 'the' with a masculine noun, then 'to be' for origin.
Masculine 'the' is *el*; 'is' (he/it) is *es*. Origin uses *de* + the country.
*El señor ___ de Argentina* — fill in the *él* form of *ser*.

sentences.es: Me llamo Diego y soy de Colombia.
sentences.en: My name is Diego and I'm from Colombia.
acceptedEs: Yo me llamo Diego y soy de Colombia.
Me llamo Diego y yo soy de Colombia.
Yo me llamo Diego y yo soy de Colombia.
Soy Diego y soy de Colombia.
acceptedEn: My name is Diego and I am from Colombia.
hints: Give your name with the set phrase, then add where you're from with *ser*.
'My name is' is the fixed *me llamo*; 'I'm from' is *soy de*.
*Me llamo Diego y ___ de Colombia* — fill in the *yo* form of *ser*.
Use 'the' for a feminine noun, then 'to be' for origin.
Feminine 'the' is *la*; 'is' is *es*. Origin uses *de*.
*___ señora es de Colombia* — fill in feminine 'the.'

sentences.es: Buenos días. Me llamo Diego y soy de Perú.
sentences.en: Good morning. My name is Diego and I'm from Peru.
acceptedEs: Buenos días. Yo me llamo Diego y soy de Perú.
Buenos días. Me llamo Diego y yo soy de Perú.
Buenos días. Yo me llamo Diego y yo soy de Perú.
Buen día. Me llamo Diego y soy de Perú.
acceptedEn: Good morning. My name is Diego and I am from Peru.
hints: Open with a morning greeting, give your name, then your origin.
'Good morning' is *buenos días*; use the fixed *me llamo* and *soy de* for origin.
*Buenos días. Me llamo Diego y ___ de Perú* — fill in the *yo* form of *ser*.

sentences.es: Ella se llama Sofía y es de Perú.
sentences.en: Her name is Sofía and she's from Peru.
acceptedEs: Se llama Sofía y es de Perú.
Es de Perú y se llama Sofía.
Ella es de Perú y se llama Sofía.
acceptedEn: Her name is Sofia and she is from Peru.
hints: Say her name with the third-person set phrase, then her origin.
'Her name is' is the fixed *se llama*; 'she's from' is *es de*.
*Ella ___ Sofía y es de Perú* — fill in the set phrase for 'is called.'

acceptedEs: Buenas noches. Yo soy de México.
Buenas noches, soy de México.
Buenas noches, yo soy de México.
acceptedEn: Good evening. I am from Mexico.
hints: Open with an evening greeting, then say where you're from.
'Good evening' is *buenas noches*; 'I'm from' is *soy de*.
*Buenas noches. ___ de México* — fill in the *yo* form of *ser*.

sentences.es: Yo soy de México y tú eres de Chile.
sentences.en: I'm from Mexico and you're from Chile.
acceptedEs: Soy de México y eres de Chile.
Soy de México y tú eres de Chile.
Yo soy de México y eres de Chile.
acceptedEn: I am from Mexico and you are from Chile.
hints: Two people: give your origin, then the other person's, keeping both subjects.
'I am' is *soy*, 'you are' is *eres*; both use *de* for origin.
*Yo soy de México y tú ___ de Chile* — fill in the *tú* form of *ser*.

acceptedEs: Muchas gracias, señor.
Señor, gracias.
¡Gracias, señor!
hints: Thank someone, then address a man politely.
'Thank you' is one word; the polite word for a man is *señor*.
*___, señor* — fill in 'thank you.'

acceptedEs: Señora, perdón.
¡Perdón, señora!
hints: Apologize or excuse yourself, then address a woman politely.
The apology word starts with *p*; the polite word for a woman is *señora*.
*___, señora* — fill in the apology word.

acceptedEs: Señor, por favor.
¡Por favor, señor!
hints: Say 'please,' then address a man politely.
'Please' is a two-word phrase; the polite word for a man is *señor*.
*___, señor* — fill in the two-word phrase for 'please.'

acceptedEs: Señora, adiós.
¡Adiós, señora!
hints: Say goodbye, then address a woman politely.
'Goodbye' starts with *a*; the polite word for a woman is *señora*.
*___, señora* — fill in 'goodbye.'

sentences.es: Yo me llamo Ana y tú te llamas Pedro.
sentences.en: My name is Ana and your name is Pedro.
acceptedEs: Me llamo Ana y te llamas Pedro.
Me llamo Ana y tú te llamas Pedro.
Yo me llamo Ana y te llamas Pedro.
acceptedEn: My name is Ana and your name's Pedro.
hints: Give your name, then the other person's, using the two set phrases.
'My name is' is *me llamo*; 'your name is' is *te llamas*.
*Yo me llamo Ana y tú ___ Pedro* — fill in the 'your name is' phrase.

sentences.es: Nosotros somos de Colombia y ellos son de México.
sentences.en: We're from Colombia and they're from Mexico.
acceptedEs: Somos de Colombia y son de México.
Somos de Colombia y ellos son de México.
Nosotros somos de Colombia y son de México.
Nosotras somos de Colombia y ellas son de México.
acceptedEn: We are from Colombia and they are from Mexico.
hints: Two groups: 'we' and 'they,' each with their origin.
'We are' is *somos*; 'they are' is *son*; both use *de*.
*Nosotros somos de Colombia y ellos ___ de México* — fill in the *ellos* form of *ser*.

conversation.scenario: Meeting someone new at a language exchange.
conversation.personaPrompt: You are Camila, a friendly student from Mexico. Speak only in short, present-tense Spanish sentences using this lesson's greetings, ser, and me llamo / se llama. Use tú with the learner, never vosotros, and no slang. Introduce yourself first, then let the learner introduce themselves back declaratively (no questions — question words come later).
conversation.openingLine: Hola, me llamo Camila. Soy de México.
conversation.openingLineGloss: Hi, my name is Camila. I'm from Mexico.

quickChecks.explanation: Use soy, the yo form of ser, to say where you're from.
Señora is feminine singular, so it takes la.

quickChecks.prompt: In the introduction card, where is Camila from?
